prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength made atomic timekeeping at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B027, Katori and Ye. The physics can be told in one picture. At the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts the two clock levels by the same amount, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held still and interrogated together, free of Doppler and recoil broadening and with a large atom number. That is a new regime of control, and it has been delivered as a measurement: independent lattice clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere agree near 1e-18, which is the kind of reproducibility I weigh above all. The consequences follow from the science: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter limits on varying constants, many-body and spin-exchange physics inside the lattice, and a firm basis for the redefinition of the second. The round 1 exchange has not weakened this. Six of eight members now name it first, and the support comes from people in very different fields. No other entry has an attribution that is as settled. I would word the citation as invention and development, as Olsson asked, so that Katori's magic-wavelength concept and first strontium realisation and Ye's record accuracy and many-body work are each described correctly.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still novelty relative to 2005 (the comb) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems and ion clocks), and I cannot claim the objection is empty. My answer is that neither of those prizes covers neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, which is a different mechanism with a different precision regime, but a reasonable colleague could weigh it the other way. Second, the discovery content is a capability and its demonstrated yield, not yet a surprise from nature; the variation-of-constants and dark-matter results so far are limits. Third, a two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow, Takamoto and others, and Ye's own claim is development rather than the original idea. I also note once more that I am an atomic theorist and may find this case more natural than colleagues from other fields would.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the Takamoto, Ludlow and Hall contributions create a real attribution problem, whether Ye's role is development of Katori's concept, and says the citation should say invention and development and rest on demonstrated accuracy rather than on promised applications.
responses.response: I agree with your wording and would make it the committee's. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock are the original invention. Ye's claim is the decisive development: the accuracy and stability frontier, the clock comparisons and the many-body physics in the lattice. That is a legitimate second name provided the citation says invention and development. On your direct question, I think Takamoto and Ludlow are a footnote and not a disturbance: they demonstrated and refined the clock in Katori's and Ye's groups, so their work lies inside the two credited lineages, and the Lemonde and Derevianko contributions are important but are not a competing invention of the magic-wavelength lattice. I would rest the citation on the 1e-18 comparisons and not on geodesy or dark-matter searches, which are still promises. Your move from B053 to this entry is not what I would call a concession by an interested party; it is the standard you apply to your own field.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B057 as the entry with a new organising principle, answers the 2016 overlap by distinguishing model topology from time-reversal-invariant band insulators in real materials, concedes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap, and says he would move the clock to the top if that credit question stays unsettled.
responses.response: Your answer on 2016 persuades me more than it did in round 1: a classification of real band insulators with a decisive measurement is more than a repeat. It also helps that you hold the condensed-matter judgement, which I do not. Where we still differ is the weighing. You value a new organising principle above a new precision regime; I accept that as a serious criterion, and I keep B057 as my first alternative for exactly that reason. But you describe the credit gap as the real weakness, and I would add that the committee cannot repair it. Zhang is deceased, so the omission is permanent, and a Z2 and HgTe citation would have to explain it every time it is read. By your own conditional the clock should lead this year. I would not oppose B057 in a later cycle if the committee can state the Kane-Mele proposal and Molenkamp measurement as the core in a way that does not suggest the HgTe prediction is unrecognised.

responses.point: Danielsson moved the clock from third to first, wants the citation to say what the precision has already shown (millimetre redshift tests, many-body clock physics) so that it does not read as a third award for better clocks, and doubts atom interferometry and the Higgs credit.
responses.response: I agree, and I take your request seriously because it answers the objection most likely to be raised against us. My citation names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping, and the 10^-18 level, and I would add a sentence in the committee's popular text on gravitational redshift over millimetres and many-body clock physics, since these are what the precision has already shown. I also agree on B032: Chu's 1997 prize and his light-pulse gravimeter make a Borde-Pritchard-Kasevich trio awkward, and I have lowered it for that reason, so I keep B057 and B053 as my alternatives. On IceCube I take your point that it opens a new window, but I stay cautious about naming two individuals for a roughly 300-person collaboration result when source identification is still incomplete.

responses.point: Johansson argues that the cancellation of light shifts is itself the discovery, that the 2005 and 2012 prizes made the clock possible but do not cover neutral atoms in a lattice, and says he should weigh his own vote carefully on B036 while dropping his first choice.
responses.response: I welcome your reasoning and I value that you moved off B036 on the grounds of proximity and the 2025 prize. I agree that the point is the lattice and the light-shift cancellation, and I accept your qualification that the citation should not read as a comb or ion-clock prize extended. We differ in one respect: you read the earlier prizes as precedent that cuts mildly in our favour, while I regard it as an open question that the committee should say it has examined. I am less sure than you that the question is closed, which is why I list it under uncertainties. I also agree with you against widening the credit to Zoller or to comb-clock coupling: it would blur a clean pair.

responses.point: Mehlig regards B027 as a fully legitimate winner with the best attribution and timing, but would not let a clean credit decide the matter, since a clean credit partly reflects a technique with few people, and ranks B057 first for its combination of decisive theory and decisive experiment.
responses.response: I agree that clean attribution is not by itself a reason to give a prize, and I do not rest on it. My reason is the combination of a new regime of control, independent verification at 1e-18, and demonstrated scientific yield. The clean credit follows from that. I also appreciate that you say you could not make a scientific case against B027. For B057 I accept your framing around the Z2 concept and observation, and your request to Eriksson to show that the citation does not imply the HgTe prediction is unrecognised is the right test. I do not regard that test as passed yet.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge it distinct, but I cannot prove it.
Whether the redefinition of the second should come first. I think the science is mature without it, but waiting one cycle would cost little if the committee prefers that.

Whether a third contributor such as Lemonde or Derevianko has a priority claim strong enough to disturb the two-name credit, and the priority between lattice clocks and single-ion optical clocks, which I cannot resolve from the files.
Whether B057 can be resolved against the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and three-dimensional credit problem, which I cannot judge from outside condensed matter.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, and have worked with Lund and ETH attosecond groups; this does not involve Katori or Ye, and I know of no personal or institutional connection to either of them or to any other credited person on the shortlist. I work in atomic theory in the same broad field as the clock candidate, which may bias me toward it, and I state that openly. No disclosure has changed since round 1, and none requires recusal.
